message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, no mold, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If the landlord fails to fix a serious issue, you may withhold rent or repair‑and‑deduct (but only after giving notice). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice if you’re not sure. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the term ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the court process: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days) for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend any court hearing; you can present evidence of your compliance or any landlord misconduct. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to repair a problem and deduct the cost from rent **only** if the landlord fails to fix it after notice. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • If you feel your privacy is violated, document the incident and consider filing a complaint. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Generally allowed if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission; subletting without consent can be grounds for eviction. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must maintain common areas (hallways, elevators, parking). | • Report issues promptly. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required, having a written lease protects both parties. | • Always read the lease carefully; ask questions before signing. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease in full.** Look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask about utilities and who pays them.** 3. **Confirm the security deposit amount** and the conditions for its return. 4. **Check for any “no‑cure‑no‑pay” clauses** that might waive your right to repair‑and‑deduct. 5. **Verify the landlord’s contact information** and how they prefer to receive notices. 6. **Document the unit’s condition** with photos and a written move‑in inspection. ### Resources | Resource | What it offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Tenant‑rights guides, dispute resolution tips. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Local tenant‑rights groups** (e.g., Houston Tenants Union, Dallas Housing Rights) | Legal clinics, workshops. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair Housing resources. | | **Legal Aid of Texas** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | --- #### Bottom line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely return of your security deposit, reasonable notice before landlord entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear path to challenge unlawful eviction or repairs. Keeping thorough records, communicating in writing, and knowing the basic statutes above will help you protect those rights.
